{"body":"A second full game — *NFs, Please!*, a Papers-Please-style business sim about a Brazilian
finance analyst — was built on MonoDreams: desktop + web
(KNI/BlazorGL) heads, published to itch.io, ~1.6k unit tests, fully agent-validated via
scripted-cursor runs and screenshot reads. Where #35 (Witch v Necromancer) exercised the
platformer muscle (physics, LDtk worlds, editor), this game exercises the **business-UI
muscle**: `ui`, `rendering-text`, `cursor`, mouse-first interaction, window/pane management,
BlazorGL content, and long unattended agentic runs.

One fact makes this catalogue different from #35: **zero vendored-module `.cs` files were
edited** — a hard rule enforced across every development wave. Everything below is therefore
(a) an upstream bug found and worked around game-side, (b) a CLI/template gap that cost real
effort, or (c) a game-side system deliberately built engine-shaped, ready to lift.

---

## A. Upstream bugs

### A1. `collision` module manifest omits its real `physics` dependency
`monodreams add collision` (without `physics`) produces a project that does not compile:
`collision/System/ColliderBody.cs` and `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem.cs` import
`MonoDreams.Component.Physics`, but `module.json` declares `deps: foundation` only — and the
CLI's own `list` output advertises "soft-couples to physics". Workaround: install `physics`
even though the game never registers its systems.
**Fix options:** declare the dep, or split the physics-coupled files into an optional part.
**Generalization (tooling):** the CLI could validate every manifest by compiling each module
against its declared deps only — this whole bug class becomes CI-detectable.

### A2. `init` template collides `<Game>.Game` namespace with `Xna.Framework.Game` (CS0118)
Any scaffolded game that creates a `<RootNamespace>.Game.*` namespace (a natural choice)
breaks the unqualified `Game` base-class reference in **two CLI-emitted files**: `GameRoot.cs`
and the web head's `Pages/Index.razor.cs` (`private Game _game`). Member-of-namespace wins
over using-directives in the enclosing-namespace walk; a global using alias does NOT fix it
(verified empirically). It bit this project twice, weeks apart, because the web head is not
in the default solution build.
**Fix:** fully qualify `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Game` in both template files.

### A3. Windowed games larger than the display render offscreen (macOS)
MonoGame 3.8.4 DesktopGL: a **fixed** window is *not* clamped by macOS (a resizable one is),
so `PreferredBackBuffer = 1920x1080` on a 1512x982-pt MacBook opens a window bigger than the
screen. MonoGame also doesn't bind `SDL_GetDisplayUsableBounds` (menu-bar-aware area), only
`GetBounds`/`GetCurrentDisplayMode`. Game-side fix worth lifting into `foundation` or the
head template — `NfsPlease.Core/WindowFit.cs` + `DesktopWindow.cs`:
- largest aspect-correct window inside the *usable* bounds (direct `SDL_GetDisplayUsableBounds`
  export call on the SDL MonoGame already loaded; fixed-margin fallback), snapped to
  multiples of 16, capped at the render resolution (1:1 = sharpest);
- resizable in human modes; fixed in override/pin modes;
- `NFS_WINDOW=WxH` env override; a *screenshot-pin* mode (see C3);
- boot log line of display/usable/window/mode — the feature's observable.
Empirical notes worth keeping wherever this lands: everything (display mode, SDL window,
GL backbuffer) is in **points** on macOS DesktopGL — no Retina conversion anywhere.

---

## B. CLI / template gaps

### B1. Scaffolded web head ships a "CONTENT BUILD (not wired)" placeholder
Wiring BlazorGL content on macOS means hand-porting from `MonoDreams.Demos.Web.csproj`:
`KniContentBuilderExe=dotnet`, the FreeImage/freetype native shim staged from `dotnet-mgcb`,
`KNI.Extended(.Content.Pipeline)`+`Autofac` staging, ffmpeg/ffprobe staging for `.wav`, and
`KniContentReference`. All of it is boilerplate identical across games (this game needed zero
game-specific deviation — only prebuilt KNI.Extended importers, no source-built pipeline
dlls). The CLI template could emit the whole block; games with source-built pipeline dlls
add the extra target later.

### B2. `add`/`init` UX nit
`monodreams add --project` vs `init --dir` for "where is the project" — same concept, two
option names; `add rendering --dir x` silently parses `--dir` as a module name and fails with
a confusing "Module '--dir' not found".

---

## C. Lift-ready game-side systems

### C1. Two coordinate spaces: authoring vs render (`Game/Screens/RenderSpace.cs`)
The game went 720p→1080p with a ~90-line diff and **zero test/coordinate recalibration**:
authoring stays in `LayoutWidth/Height` (all game numbers), render targets/backbuffer use
`VirtualWidth/Height`, and the scale lives in exactly one place — per-pass render cameras
(engine contract "camera virtual resolution == destination size" holds) plus a `MapMouse`
that inverts the present `DestinationRectangle` (robust to resize/letterbox). Bonus: bitmap
glyphs rasterize through the camera, so text gains real fidelity from the same masters.
`ViewportManager` half-supports this today; making the two-space model first-class in
`rendering` (or a documented pattern + helpers) would give every game cheap resolution moves.

### C2. Per-layer present sampler (`Game/Screens/PresentLayers.cs`)
Engine presents UI/HUD with `PointClamp`; at non-integer downscale (window < render res) UI
text shimmers. The game-side seam: point when scale == 1, linear otherwise, per layer —
`RenderLayer` is a public record, so screens own the list. Engine could carry a sampler
policy on `RenderLayer` (or auto-select by scale) and delete this seam.

### C3. Scripted-pointer driver + fixed-size screenshot capture (the agentic loop)
The single highest-leverage tool of the whole project. Engine's `input_replay.json` drives
*named actions* only — useless for a mouse game. The game grew an env-gated driver
(`DeskDriverSystem` and friends): staged scripts of cursor moves/clicks/wheel/typed-text,
`waitUntil`-style stage gating, per-scenario modes, and every wave validated itself by
running scenarios headed + reading the PNGs. Two engine-worthy pieces:
- a generic **PointerReplaySystem** in `debug` (JSON: move/click/wheel/type/waitUntil/label),
  sharing the replay philosophy of input_replay but for the pointer;
- **`ScreenshotCaptureSystem` reads the window backbuffer**, so PNG size follows the window.
  For stable agentic evidence the game pins the window when screenshots are on
  ("screenshot-pin"). Better upstream: an option to capture a named RenderTarget at its
  fixed resolution, independent of window size.
Related field note for `debug` docs: on macOS, unattended runs need `caffeinate -disu` —
App Nap/display sleep freezes the loop (one 3h run hung inside `Cocoa_GL_SwapWindow`); an
opt-in `MONODREAMS_KEEP_AWAKE=1` (NSProcessInfo activity) would remove the footgun.

### C4. Font-aware text sanitization for BitmapFonts (`Game/UI/UiKit.ForDisplay/ForMono`)
Bitmap faces have partial glyph coverage (one face here lacks em-dash/ordinals; the mono face
is caps-only, no diacritics). Naive rendering silently drops glyphs mid-word. The game-side
pipeline: per-face whitelist read from the `.fnt`, deterministic folds (— → -, º → o,
… → ..., diacritic strip + upcase for the caps face), silent-drop as a *tested, intentional*
behavior. `rendering-text` could expose glyph-coverage queries + a fold hook, and warn at
prep time on missing glyphs — today the failure is invisible.

### C5. Entity highlight overlay (`Game/System/TutorialGlowSystem.cs`)
Generic pulsing outline attached to ANY entity (papers, text hotspots, buttons, taskbar
icons): parented so it follows transforms, re-derives depth per frame (survives z restacks),
dies with its target. Built for the tutorial; useful for any onboarding/debug highlighting.
Natural home: `ui` or `debug`.

### C6. Small `ui` module gaps filled game-side
- **PinnedLayoutRootComponent/System**: `AutoLayoutBuilder` anchors roots to screen edges and
  stacks multiple roots in the implicit solver container — you can't pin N independent roots
  at arbitrary positions. The game's pin system (post-AutoLayout, pre-Hierarchy) is the same
  seam the engine's own demo uses ad hoc.
- **TooltipSystem**: one-line floating tooltip riding the pointer pick — no primitive today.
- **Tab-content parking**: the ScrollView/tab premise ("park, don't hide") is easy to get
  wrong; a `TabSystem` helper for parking off-screen would encode it.

---

## D. Pattern lessons (docs material, no code to lift)

- **Physical-layer vs `UIFocusSystem` double-dispatch**: any game mixing world picking with
  the `ui` module needs an explicit arbitration (this game: focus groups + a gate system that
  disables UIFocus on frames the physical layer owns the pointer). Worth a premises note in
  `ui` — the failure mode (click leaks through a paper into a tab underneath) is silent.
- **Message-driven audio cues**: one `AudioCueSystem` subscribing to existing gameplay
  messages → `PlaySoundRequest` kept audio fully decoupled; zero `Play` calls inside game
  systems. Good candidate for an `audio` docs example.
- The **two-space + scripted-driver + RT-screenshot** trio is what made ~15 waves of
  agent-implemented, agent-verified development possible. If MonoDreams wants "AI-agent
  friendly" as a headline feature (README says it does), C1+C3 are the highest-leverage
  investments in this list.

---

Sub-issues: to be split by the owner (as agreed) — this issue is the catalogue and the
ranking conversation.
","labels":[],"title":"Upstreaming NFs, Please!: engine bugs, template gaps and lift-ready systems from a business-UI game on MonoDreams","url":"https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/issues/81"}

**Fix options:** declare the dep, or split the physics-coupled files into an optional part.
**Generalization (tooling):** the CLI could validate every manifest by compiling each module
against its declared deps only — this whole bug class becomes CI-detectable.

### A2. `init` template collides `<Game>.Game` namespace with `Xna.Framework.Game` (CS0118)
Any scaffolded game that creates a `<RootNamespace>.Game.*` namespace (a natural choice)
breaks the unqualified `Game` base-class reference in **two CLI-emitted files**: `GameRoot.cs`
and the web head's `Pages/Index.razor.cs` (`private Game _game`). Member-of-namespace wins
over using-directives in the enclosing-namespace walk; a global using alias does NOT fix it
(verified empirically). It bit this project twice, weeks apart, because the web head is not
in the default solution build.
**Fix:** fully qualify `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Game` in both template files.

### A3. Windowed games larger than the display render offscreen (macOS)
MonoGame 3.8.4 DesktopGL: a **fixed** window is *not* clamped by macOS (a resizable one is),
so `PreferredBackBuffer = 1920x1080` on a 1512x982-pt MacBook opens a window bigger than the
screen. MonoGame also doesn't bind `SDL_GetDisplayUsableBounds` (menu-bar-aware area), only
`GetBounds`/`GetCurrentDisplayMode`. Game-side fix worth lifting into `foundation` or the
head template — `NfsPlease.Core/WindowFit.cs` + `DesktopWindow.cs`:
- largest aspect-correct window inside the *usable* bounds (direct `SDL_GetDisplayUsableBounds`
  export call on the SDL MonoGame already loaded; fixed-margin fallback), snapped to
  multiples of 16, capped at the render resolution (1:1 = sharpest);
- resizable in human modes; fixed in override/pin modes;
- `NFS_WINDOW=WxH` env override; a *screenshot-pin* mode (see C3);
- boot log line of display/usable/window/mode — the feature's observable.
Empirical notes worth keeping wherever this lands: everything (display mode, SDL window,
GL backbuffer) is in **points** on macOS DesktopGL — no Retina conversion anywhere.

---

## B. CLI / template gaps

### B1. Scaffolded web head ships a "CONTENT BUILD (not wired)" placeholder
Wiring BlazorGL content on macOS means hand-porting from `MonoDreams.Demos.Web.csproj`:
`KniContentBuilderExe=dotnet`, the FreeImage/freetype native shim staged from `dotnet-mgcb`,
`KNI.Extended(.Content.Pipeline)`+`Autofac` staging, ffmpeg/ffprobe staging for `.wav`, and
`KniContentReference`. All of it is boilerplate identical across games (this game needed zero
game-specific deviation — only prebuilt KNI.Extended importers, no source-built pipeline
dlls). The CLI template could emit the whole block; games with source-built pipeline dlls
add the extra target later.

### B2. `add`/`init` UX nit
`monodreams add --project` vs `init --dir` for "where is the project" — same concept, two
option names; `add rendering --dir x` silently parses `--dir` as a module name and fails with
a confusing "Module '--dir' not found".

---

## C. Lift-ready game-side systems

### C1. Two coordinate spaces: authoring vs render (`Game/Screens/RenderSpace.cs`)
The game went 720p→1080p with a ~90-line diff and **zero test/coordinate recalibration**:
authoring stays in `LayoutWidth/Height` (all game numbers), render targets/backbuffer use
`VirtualWidth/Height`, and the scale lives in exactly one place — per-pass render cameras
(engine contract "camera virtual resolution == destination size" holds) plus a `MapMouse`
that inverts the present `DestinationRectangle` (robust to resize/letterbox). Bonus: bitmap
glyphs rasterize through the camera, so text gains real fidelity from the same masters.
`ViewportManager` half-supports this today; making the two-space model first-class in
`rendering` (or a documented pattern + helpers) would give every game cheap resolution moves.

### C2. Per-layer present sampler (`Game/Screens/PresentLayers.cs`)
Engine presents UI/HUD with `PointClamp`; at non-integer downscale (window < render res) UI
text shimmers. The game-side seam: point when scale == 1, linear otherwise, per layer —
`RenderLayer` is a public record, so screens own the list. Engine could carry a sampler
policy on `RenderLayer` (or auto-select by scale) and delete this seam.

### C3. Scripted-pointer driver + fixed-size screenshot capture (the agentic loop)
The single highest-leverage tool of the whole project. Engine's `input_replay.json` drives
*named actions* only — useless for a mouse game. The game grew an env-gated driver
(`DeskDriverSystem` and friends): staged scripts of cursor moves/clicks/wheel/typed-text,
`waitUntil`-style stage gating, per-scenario modes, and every wave validated itself by
running scenarios headed + reading the PNGs. Two engine-worthy pieces:
- a generic **PointerReplaySystem** in `debug` (JSON: move/click/wheel/type/waitUntil/label),
  sharing the replay philosophy of input_replay but for the pointer;
- **`ScreenshotCaptureSystem` reads the window backbuffer**, so PNG size follows the window.
  For stable agentic evidence the game pins the window when screenshots are on
  ("screenshot-pin"). Better upstream: an option to capture a named RenderTarget at its
  fixed resolution, independent of window size.
Related field note for `debug` docs: on macOS, unattended runs need `caffeinate -disu` —
App Nap/display sleep freezes the loop (one 3h run hung inside `Cocoa_GL_SwapWindow`); an
opt-in `MONODREAMS_KEEP_AWAKE=1` (NSProcessInfo activity) would remove the footgun.

### C4. Font-aware text sanitization for BitmapFonts (`Game/UI/UiKit.ForDisplay/ForMono`)
Bitmap faces have partial glyph coverage (one face here lacks em-dash/ordinals; the mono face
is caps-only, no diacritics). Naive rendering silently drops glyphs mid-word. The game-side
pipeline: per-face whitelist read from the `.fnt`, deterministic folds (— → -, º → o,
… → ..., diacritic strip + upcase for the caps face), silent-drop as a *tested, intentional*
behavior. `rendering-text` could expose glyph-coverage queries + a fold hook, and warn at
prep time on missing glyphs — today the failure is invisible.

### C5. Entity highlight overlay (`Game/System/TutorialGlowSystem.cs`)
Generic pulsing outline attached to ANY entity (papers, text hotspots, buttons, taskbar
icons): parented so it follows transforms, re-derives depth per frame (survives z restacks),
dies with its target. Built for the tutorial; useful for any onboarding/debug highlighting.
Natural home: `ui` or `debug`.

### C6. Small `ui` module gaps filled game-side
- **PinnedLayoutRootComponent/System**: `AutoLayoutBuilder` anchors roots to screen edges and
  stacks multiple roots in the implicit solver container — you can't pin N independent roots
  at arbitrary positions. The game's pin system (post-AutoLayout, pre-Hierarchy) is the same
  seam the engine's own demo uses ad hoc.
- **TooltipSystem**: one-line floating tooltip riding the pointer pick — no primitive today.
- **Tab-content parking**: the ScrollView/tab premise ("park, don't hide") is easy to get
  wrong; a `TabSystem` helper for parking off-screen would encode it.

---

## D. Pattern lessons (docs material, no code to lift)

- **Physical-layer vs `UIFocusSystem` double-dispatch**: any game mixing world picking with
  the `ui` module needs an explicit arbitration (this game: focus groups + a gate system that
  disables UIFocus on frames the physical layer owns the pointer). Worth a premises note in
  `ui` — the failure mode (click leaks through a paper into a tab underneath) is silent.
- **Message-driven audio cues**: one `AudioCueSystem` subscribing to existing gameplay
  messages → `PlaySoundRequest` kept audio fully decoupled; zero `Play` calls inside game
  systems. Good candidate for an `audio` docs example.
- The **two-space + scripted-driver + RT-screenshot** trio is what made ~15 waves of
  agent-implemented, agent-verified development possible. If MonoDreams wants "AI-agent
  friendly" as a headline feature (README says it does), C1+C3 are the highest-leverage
  investments in this list.

---

Sub-issues: to be split by the owner (as agreed) — this issue is the catalogue and the
ranking conversation.

content.text:
Read it — great catalogue. Here's how I'll run this: I'll first lay out my proposed split so you can see the whole map, then we go one at a time. For each sub-issue I'll give you context, a concrete "what would happen without it" picture, and my proposal; you approve/reject/adjust; on approval I create it via `gh` (as a sub-issue of #81) and move on. Open questions from the catalogue (A1's fix option, C1's "first-class vs pattern", C2's sampler policy, C3's capture design, C5's home module) get answered inline as we hit each one.

## Proposed split (13 candidate sub-issues, sequenceable)

| # | Item(s) | One-liner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A1 | `collision` module manifest: fix the missing `physics` dep |
| 2 | A1-gen | CLI/CI: compile each module against its declared deps only (kills the whole bug class) |
| 3 | A2 | Templates: fully qualify `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Game` (CS0118 trap) |
| 4 | B2 | CLI UX: unify `--project`/`--dir`, error loudly on unknown options |
| 5 | A3 | Window fit: usable-bounds-aware, aspect-correct windowing in `foundation`/template |
| 6 | B1 | Web head template: emit the full BlazorGL content-build block |
| 7 | C1 | Two coordinate spaces (authoring vs render) as a first-class `rendering` concern |
| 8 | C2 | Per-layer present sampler policy on `RenderLayer` |
| 9 | C3a | `PointerReplaySystem` in `debug` (mouse-game replay) |
| 10 | C3b | RenderTarget-resolution screenshot capture + `MONODREAMS_KEEP_AWAKE` |
| 11 | C4 | `rendering-text`: glyph-coverage queries, fold hook, prep-time missing-glyph warning |
| 12 | C5 | Entity highlight/glow overlay system |
| 13 | C6 + D | `ui` gaps (pinned roots, tooltip, tab parking) + docs premises (double-dispatch, audio cues) — likely to be split further when we get there |

---

## Sub-issue 1 of 13 — A1: `collision` manifest omits its real `physics` dependency

**The picture:** imagine a newcomer building a top-down puzzle game — no gravity, no momentum, just "did the crate touch the switch". They run `monodreams add collision`, exactly what the docs suggest. The build immediately fails with errors about `MonoDreams.Component.Physics` — a namespace from a module they never installed and don't want. Their first five minutes with the engine end in a compiler error caused by *our* metadata, and the "fix" (install physics they'll never register) teaches them the manifests can't be trusted. For a shadcn-style engine whose whole pitch is "add a module and it just works", a module that doesn't compile after `add` is the pitch failing at hello-world.

**Why it happens:** `ColliderBody.cs` and `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem.cs` import physics types, but `module.json` declares only `foundation`. The docs even say "soft-couples to physics" — but the coupling is compile-time hard.

**My proposal:** make the manifest honest — declare `physics` as a dep. I'd *not* go for the file-split option (carving the physics-coupled resolution files into an optional sub-part) right now: it's a real design change to the module system (partial modules don't exist yet), and the practical cost of pulling in `physics` sources you don't register is near zero — dormant source files, shadcn-style. If "collision without physics" ever becomes a real demand, the split can be its own issue then. This keeps sub-issue 1 a small, immediately shippable correctness fix.

**Value:** `monodreams add collision` compiles, first-run trust restored, and the CLI's `list` output stops advertising something false.

errors about a namespace from a module they never installed.

- Add `physics` to `deps` in `MonoDreams/collision/module.json`.

detection works without `physics`) was considered and deferred — partial modules don't
exist in the module system today, and pulling in dormant `physics` sources costs users
nothing. If "collision without physics" becomes a real demand, that split is its own issue.

## Sub-issue 2 of 13 — A1-generalization: CI that catches lying manifests automatically

**What it's about:** #82 fixed the one manifest we *know* was wrong (`collision` hiding its `physics` dep) — but nothing prevents the next one. This sub-issue builds the tooling that makes the whole bug class impossible to ship again.

**The picture:** think of each `module.json` deps list as a recipe's ingredient list. Nobody ever cooks a recipe using *only* its listed ingredients — every dev machine and every test run has all 13 modules sitting in the pantry, so a missing ingredient never gets noticed. That's exactly why the collision bug survived for months: it could only manifest on a *fresh user's* machine, right after `monodreams add collision` — the worst person to find it (a newcomer), at the worst moment (their first five minutes). Any future refactor that adds a cross-module `using` will silently corrupt another manifest in the same invisible way.

**My proposal — literally cook each recipe as written:**

1. For each of the 13 modules: scaffold a temp project, run `monodreams add <module>` (which installs the module plus its *declared* transitive deps and nothing else), then `dotnet build`.
2. Any build failure means either the manifest lies or `add` itself is broken — both things you want to know before a user does.
3. Ship it as a runnable test suite / CLI check, and wire it into GitHub Actions for PRs touching `MonoDreams/` or `MonoDreams.Cli/`.

**Value:** manifests stop being hopeful documentation and become CI-verified contracts — and `monodreams add` gets its first real end-to-end CI coverage for free. Cost: ~13 small builds per CI run, parallelizable.

**Sequencing:** depends on #82 — which is actually a nice birth test: the check should fail on pre-#82 code and go green after, proving it detects the real bug.

---

## Sub-issue 3 of 13 — A2: templates break when your game has a `Game` namespace (CS0118)

**The picture:** you scaffold a new game called `NfsPlease` and, like any sane developer, organize your code as `NfsPlease.Game.Screens`, `NfsPlease.Game.Systems` — "Game" is the most natural folder name in a game project. The moment you do, two files *the CLI itself generated* stop compiling: `GameRoot.cs` and the web head's `Index.razor.cs` both reference the base class as bare `Game`, and C#'s name resolution now finds your *namespace* `NfsPlease.Game` before it finds `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Game` — "'Game' is a namespace but is used like a type" (CS0118). It's a trap the template digs and the user falls into, with a cryptic error pointing at code they didn't write.

**Why it's nastier than it looks:** it bit *NFs, Please!* **twice, weeks apart** — because the web head isn't in the default solution build, so fixing `GameRoot.cs` doesn't reveal the identical landmine in `Index.razor.cs` until you next build for web. And the "obvious" fix (a global using alias) empirically does *not* work — member-of-namespace lookup wins over using-directives, so only full qualification saves you.

**My proposal:** a tiny, surgical template fix — in both CLI-emitted files, replace the bare `Game` references with fully-qualified `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Game`. Optionally add a template-scaffold test that creates a project with a `<Root>.Game` namespace and builds both heads, so the trap can't be re-dug.

**Value:** the single most natural namespace choice in a game project stops breaking scaffolded games. Two-line fix, zero risk, pure first-impression win.

Approve / reject / comment?

## Sub-issue 7 of 13 — C1: make the two-coordinate-space model (authoring vs render) first-class in `rendering`

**The picture:** imagine writing a book where every measurement is in "final printed inches". The day the publisher switches from paperback to hardcover, you re-edit every page. That's how most games hardcode coordinates: buttons at `(1720, 980)`, tests asserting pixel positions — and a resolution change means recalibrating *everything*, including every test an agent wrote. Now the alternative: you write the book in manuscript units and only the *printer* knows the paper size. That's what NFs, Please! did — and the proof is brutal: the game moved **720p → 1080p with a ~90-line diff and zero test or coordinate recalibration**.

**How it works (`RenderSpace.cs`, proven):** all game numbers live in authoring space (`LayoutWidth/Height`); render targets and backbuffer use `VirtualWidth/Height`; and the scale between them lives in *exactly one place* — the per-pass render cameras (the existing engine contract "camera virtual resolution == destination size" already holds). Mouse input comes back through a `MapMouse` that inverts the present `DestinationRectangle`, so it's robust to window resize and letterboxing for free. Bonus: bitmap glyphs rasterize *through* the camera, so text actually gains fidelity at higher render res from the same font masters.

**The open question from #81 — first-class vs documented pattern:** I propose **first-class**. `ViewportManager` already half-supports this, which is the worst state — close enough that people assume it works, incomplete enough that they discover the gaps mid-project. Concretely: `rendering` owns an authoring-vs-virtual resolution concept (opt-in; single-space games just set them equal and nothing changes), ships the `MapMouse` inversion as an engine helper, and the docs get a premise naming the one-place-for-scale invariant. Demos/Examples adopt it as the reference usage.

**Value:** every game gets cheap resolution moves — and per #81's own closing note, this is one of the two highest-leverage items for the "AI-agent friendly" headline: agents write coordinate-laden tests *constantly*, and this is what keeps those tests from shattering on a resolution change.

Approve / reject / comment?

## Sub-issue 8 of 13 — C2: per-layer present sampler policy (kill the shimmering UI text)

**The picture:** render your game at 1080p, and the player's window happens to be 1512 px wide — a downscale of ×0.7875. The engine presents every layer with `PointClamp` (nearest-neighbor). At non-integer scale, nearest-neighbor means each screen pixel picks whichever source pixel it lands closest to — so a 1-px-wide letter stem lands on 1 screen pixel here, 2 there, and *shifts* as things move. Result: UI text visibly **shimmers and crawls**. It's the same reason a finely striped shirt strobes on camera. Point sampling is exactly right at 1:1 (crisp pixels), and exactly wrong at fractional scale (where linear sampling looks stable and clean).

**What the game did (the seam to delete):** `PresentLayers.cs` — since `RenderLayer` is a public record and screens own the list, NFs, Please! rebuilt the present pass game-side just to choose *point when scale == 1, linear otherwise, per layer*. That's a whole copy of engine plumbing maintained in a game for a one-enum decision.

**The open question from #81 — explicit policy on `RenderLayer` vs auto-select by scale: I propose both, layered.** `RenderLayer` gains a sampler policy field defaulting to `Auto` (= point at integer scale, linear otherwise — the empirically right answer, and what everyone gets for free). Games with an opinion (e.g. a deliberately chunky pixel-art layer that *wants* point even at 0.8×) set `Point` or `Linear` explicitly. The engine's present pass honors it; the game-side seam dies.

**Value:** small, sharply-scoped change to `MasterRenderSystem`'s present path; every game whose window doesn't exactly match its render resolution — which after #86 (window-fit) is *most* laptops — gets stable, readable UI text by default. Natural sequencing right after #88 since both touch the present pass.

## Sub-issue 8 (revised) — presentation scaling policy: clean scales first, samplers second

**The reframe:** shimmer is a *symptom*; the disease is being forced to present at an arbitrary fractional scale in the first place. A game should be able to declare how it wants that conflict resolved, in preference order, instead of always stretch-to-fit:

1. **Overscan to a clean scale** — the camera reveals slightly *more* world horizontally or vertically so the effective scale snaps to a friendly ratio (integer, or ½-steps). Think of a photo print: rather than squashing the photo to fit the frame, you let the frame crop/reveal a sliver more of the scene and keep the photo undistorted. Bounded by a gamedev-set tolerance (e.g. "up to 5% extra view"), because in a competitive game extra view is a gameplay decision, not just cosmetics. This composes naturally with #88's two-space model — "camera virtual resolution == destination size" is exactly the dial being turned.
2. **Letterbox / pillarbox** — keep a clean scale and pad with bars when overscan tolerance is exhausted or disabled.
3. **Stretch** (today's behavior) — and only here does the sampler question arise, resolved per layer: `Auto` (point at integer scale, linear otherwise), with explicit `Point`/`Linear` override on `RenderLayer` for opinionated layers (chunky pixel-art layer that wants point even at 0.8×).

✅ Created [#91](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/issues/91) and linked it under #81.

---

## Sub-issue 11 of 13 — C4: `rendering-text` — glyph coverage queries, fold hook, and loud missing-glyph warnings

**The picture:** bitmap fonts are stencil sets — you only own the letters you cut. Say your face has no "ã". Render `"São Paulo"` and the engine doesn't crash, doesn't warn, doesn't draw a `□` — the glyph just *silently vanishes*: the player reads **"So Paulo"**. An em-dash disappears and `"prazo — hoje"` becomes `"prazo  hoje"`. It's a typewriter with missing keys that types *nothing* when you hit one — and never tells you. Worst of all, it's invisible at dev time: your test strings happen to use covered glyphs, then real content (names, dates, a translator's ellipsis) hits production text and words quietly lose letters. In NFs, Please! one face lacked em-dash and ordinals; the mono face was caps-only with no diacritics — a Brazilian-Portuguese game on fonts that can't say "São".

**What the game built (proven):** `UiKit.ForDisplay/ForMono` — a per-face whitelist read straight from the `.fnt` file (the coverage is *right there* in the font data; the engine just never exposes it), plus deterministic folds: `—`→`-`, `º`→`o`, `…`→`...`, diacritic-strip + upcase for the caps-only face. With folds applied, silent-drop of anything *still* uncovered becomes a tested, *intentional* behavior instead of an accident.

**My proposal, three pieces in `rendering-text`:**
1. **Coverage query** — expose "does this face have this glyph / which chars of this string are missing?" from the already-parsed `.fnt` data.
2. **Fold hook** — an optional per-face transform applied before glyph layout, with the common folds shipped as ready-made building blocks (dash/ellipsis/ordinal folds, diacritic strip, upcase).
3. **Loud-by-default warning** — `TextPrepSystem` logs (once per face+char, not per frame) when it's about to drop a glyph, so the failure is visible the first time it ever happens. Games that *want* silent drop opt in.

**Value:** every text-rendering game — which is every game — stops silently corrupting words. Especially load-bearing for non-English text, and for agents: a logged warning is machine-checkable in `GameTestRunner`; a missing pixel in a word is not.

Approve / reject / comment?

## Sub-issue 12 of 13 — C5: entity highlight overlay ("point at anything" primitive)

**The picture:** every tutorial ever made needs to say *"click THIS."* The naive way is baking a glow into each thing you might point at — a glowing-button sprite variant, a glowing-paper variant… one asset and one special case per target. NFs, Please! built the general primitive instead (`TutorialGlowSystem`): attach a pulsing outline to **any** entity — a paper, a text hotspot, a button, a taskbar icon — and it just works, because it solves the three problems that make naive overlays break in an ECS:

2. **It re-derives its depth every frame**, so when z-order restacks — papers shuffling on a desk — the glow stays glued to its target instead of ending up under a sibling;
3. **It dies with its target** — no orphaned glows pulsing over empty space after the entity despawns.

Those three are exactly the invariants someone reimplementing this ad hoc gets wrong, one bug at a time.

**Open question from #81 — home: `ui` or `debug`? I propose `ui`.** It's a *player-facing* primitive (tutorials, onboarding, "quest object" hints, accessibility emphasis), and `ui` is where game-facing affordances live; `debug` is for developer instrumentation (`ColliderDebugSystem` et al.). But the component/system stays fully generic — a debug session can absolutely slap a `HighlightComponent` on an entity to eyeball it; nothing couples it to tutorials. Naming goes generic too: `HighlightComponent` + `HighlightSystem`, with pulse/color/thickness as component fields (data, not behavior — per ECS purity).

**Value:** small, self-contained, immediately usable by any game with a tutorial or hint system — and it encodes three subtle correctness invariants (follow, depth, lifetime) that would otherwise be re-discovered as three bugs per game.

## Sub-issue 13 of 16 — C6a: `PinnedLayoutRootComponent/System` — pin N independent UI roots at arbitrary positions

**The picture:** think of the auto-layout solver as a single bulletin board: everything you give `AutoLayoutBuilder` gets stacked onto that one implicit container, and roots can only anchor to screen edges. Today you *can't say that* — hand the solver three roots and it stacks them like flyers on the one board, because "several independent panels, each pinned wherever I want" has no vocabulary. **What the game proved:** a pin system that runs **post-AutoLayout, pre-Hierarchy** — let the solver do what it's good at (sizing and stacking *within* each root), then place each solved root at its pinned position before the transform hierarchy propagates. Clean separation: the solver owns *internal* layout, the pin owns *placement*.

**My proposal:** lift it into `ui` as `PinnedLayoutRootComponent` (data: anchor/offset) + a pin system slotted post-AutoLayout/pre-Hierarchy in the reference pipeline. `AutoLayoutBuilder` gets the natural entry point ("build this tree as a pinned root at P"). The demo's ad-hoc repositioning is replaced by the real thing — proof-by-dogfood in the same PR. Docs premise naming the ordering invariant (pin between AutoLayout and Hierarchy — that ordering *is* the feature).

**Value:** multi-panel screens — HUD + inventory + minimap, or any desk/dashboard layout — become declarative instead of "one solver container + hand-fixups". First of the three `ui` gaps, and the most structural.

✅ Created [#94](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/issues/94) and linked it under #81.

---

## Sub-issue 14 of 16 — C6b: `TooltipSystem` — the missing "what is this?" primitive

**The picture:** hover over anything in any desktop app — a toolbar icon, a truncated filename — and a little label materializes by the cursor. It's the cheapest affordance in all of UI: it explains without occupying space. Now count what it takes to fake one in MonoDreams today: an entity with text + background, shown/hidden by watching the pointer pick, re-positioned every frame to ride the cursor, flipped to the other side when near a screen edge (or it slides offscreen exactly when you hover the rightmost icon), drawn above everything, and torn down when the hovered thing dies. None of it is hard — all of it is fiddly, and every game re-fiddles it. NFs, Please! built exactly this once (one-line floating tooltip riding the pointer pick) and it's pure engine material: nothing in it knows about invoices or stamps.

**My proposal:** a `ui` primitive in the spirit of the module's existing pieces:
- `TooltipComponent` on any pickable entity — data only: the text (a static string first; richer content can come later without breaking the shape);
- `TooltipSystem` that rides the *existing* cursor pick (no second hit-test — the `cursor` module already knows what's under the pointer), spawns/moves the floating label, handles edge-flip, renders on the top layer, and despawns with the target or on hover-out;
- optional hover-delay field, because a tooltip that fires instantly on every pointer crossing feels like a mosquito.

**Value:** every game gets "hover to learn" for the price of one component — and it quietly raises the floor for UI-heavy games, the exact genre this whole catalogue proved the engine can serve. Also a nice showcase piece: tooltips on the engine demos' own buttons make the `ui` module feel finished.

Approve / reject / comment?

## Sub-issue 15 of 16 — C6c: `TabSystem` — encode "park, don't hide" as a reusable helper

**The picture:** tabs look trivial — "show one panel, hide the others" — and that's exactly the trap. Every developer's instinct for the inactive tab is to *hide* it (strip its visibility, stop rendering it). But the engine's own ScrollView/tab premise says the correct move is to **park** it: slide the content off-screen, alive and intact, like moving a fully-set dinner table into the next room instead of packing every dish into boxes. Hidden content goes cold — layout state, text prep, sizing all stop being maintained, and when the tab comes back you get a frame of wrong sizes, stale positions, or content that re-solves visibly in front of the player. Parked content stays warm: switch back and it's pixel-perfect instantly. The premise *exists in the docs* — but a premise you must remember mid-implementation is a bug that hasn't happened yet; NFs, Please! had to hand-build the parking dance for its window tabs, and getting it right was described as "easy to get wrong."

**My proposal:** a small `ui` helper that makes the correct thing the easy thing: a `TabGroup`-style component (data: which member is active, the park offset) + a `TabSystem` that moves inactive members to the parking position and restores the active one — so game code just flips "active tab" and never touches the parking mechanics. Reference usage in a demo, and the existing premise's `Tests:` field gets its first real test.

**Honest sizing note:** this is the smallest item in the whole catalogue — deliberately at the edge of your "too small?" criterion. I still think it stands alone because its deliverable isn't just code; it's *turning a documented footgun into an impossible mistake*, plus the premise's missing test. But folding it into #94 (as a second `ui` layout helper in one PR) would also be defensible. My lean: keep it separate — it has its own premise, its own test, its own value.

Approve as its own sub-issue / fold into #94 / reject?

---

## Sub-issue 16 of 16 — D: harvest the pattern lessons into docs (no code to lift)

Two lessons from #81's section D that are pure documentation — but each guards against a real failure mode:

**1. The pointer double-dispatch premise (`ui`).** Picture the desk in NFs, Please!: a draggable paper lying *on top of* a UI tab bar. The player clicks the paper — and the tab underneath *also* switches, because two systems answered the same click: the game's physical-layer picking and the engine's `UIFocusSystem`, each blind to the other. It's two waiters both taking the same table's order — nobody notices until two dishes arrive. The failure is completely **silent**: no error, no log, just a tab that changed when it shouldn't have — the kind of bug that ships. Any game mixing world-space picking with the `ui` module *will* hit this; the fix that worked (focus groups + a gate that disables UIFocus on frames the physical layer owns the pointer) is a pattern, and the premise to write is "one click, one owner: pointer input needs explicit arbitration between picking layers." `Tests:` starts as `none yet` honestly — this issue is about naming the invariant so implementers know arbitration is *their job*.

**2. The message-driven audio example (`audio` docs).** NFs, Please! shipped with **zero** `Play` calls inside game systems: one `AudioCueSystem` subscribed to already-existing gameplay messages (paper stamped, drawer opened) and mapped them to `PlaySoundRequest`. Audio became a pure *observer* of the game — mute it, delete it, retheme it, and no gameplay system changes; it's the film-scoring model (the composer watches the cut; the actors never play instruments) versus sound effects hardcoded into every scene's script. The `audio` module was *designed* for this (messages, `PlaySoundRequest`) but its docs never show the pattern — so users will default to sprinkling play-calls through gameplay systems, coupling what the engine took care to decouple.

**Why one sub-issue:** both are small docs edits with the same shape (harvest a proven lesson into the module docs layer) and neither justifies its own issue — this is the "join the too-small peers" case from your criteria. Delivering them means the next UI-heavy game reads its way around a silent bug and a coupling mistake instead of rediscovering both.

Approve / reject / comment?

(1) New ui premises entry, 'one click, one owner': pointer input needs explicit arbitration between world-space picking and UIFocusSystem; describe the silent failure (click leaks through a paper into a tab underneath) and the proven pattern (focus groups + a gate system disabling UIFocus on frames the physical layer owns the pointer); Tests: none yet — honestly. Follow the premises format exactly (Why/Breaks/Tests/Depends on). (2) Worked example in audio overview: an AudioCueSystem subscribing to existing gameplay messages and publishing PlaySoundRequest, stated as the recommended wiring — zero Play calls inside gameplay systems." },
]

function commonRules() {
  return [
    'IMPORTANT CONSTRAINTS:',
    "- The NFs, Please! game source referenced by the issue is NOT in this repo. Implement from the issue's design description plus existing engine code.",
    '- Components are pure data (no logic); behavior lives in systems. Prefer extending existing components/systems over creating new ones. Never create parallel render systems. One way to do things.',
    '- Match surrounding code style and idioms. Update module docs (overview/premises) when the issue calls for it — stale premises are worse than missing ones.',
    "- Build core FIRST: 'dotnet build MonoDreams/MonoDreams.csproj' — the content step references MonoDreams.dll by absolute path, so core must exist before Examples/Demos build.",
    "- Verify with the repo's configured verify command (see docs/agents/skills-config.md, section Verify). Because sibling agents run concurrently on this machine, ALWAYS pass '-m:1 -p:RestoreDisableParallel=true' to dotnet build/test to avoid NuGet restore races; on a restore flake, retry once.",
    '- Add/adjust tests per the issue (unit tests; GameTestRunner integration where applicable). All tests must pass before opening the PR.',
    '- Never push to main. Never force-push. Do not merge the PR. Keep the PR scoped to this issue only.',
  ].join('\n')
}

function implPrompt(c) {
  const branchFrom = c.stackOn
    ? "Branch setup (STACKED): run 'git fetch origin issue-" + c.stackOn + "' then 'git checkout -b issue-" + c.n + " origin/issue-" + c.stackOn + "'. If origin/issue-" + c.stackOn + " does not exist, branch from main instead and say so in notes. Create the PR with '--base issue-" + c.stackOn + "' (GitHub auto-retargets to main when the base PR merges) and mark it '--draft', noting the dependency in the body."
    : "Branch setup: 'git checkout -b issue-" + c.n + "' from current HEAD (main)."
  return [
    'You are an autonomous senior engineer implementing GitHub issue #' + c.n + ' of roo-oliv/monodreams: "' + c.title + '".',
    'You are working inside an ISOLATED GIT WORKTREE of the repo (your cwd). Do all work here.',
    '',
    'MANDATORY CONTEXT — read all of this BEFORE writing any code:',
    "1. Run 'gh issue view " + c.n + "' for the full requirements; 'gh issue view 81' for parent context if useful.",
    '2. Read docs/CORE_TENETS.md (engine-wide invariants).',
    '3. Read these load-bearing docs: ' + c.premises,
    '4. Read docs/agents/skills-config.md (verify command, commit/PR conventions).',
    '5. Study the existing code of the module(s) you will touch before deciding your design.',
    '',
    'ISSUE-SPECIFIC GUIDANCE: ' + c.extra,
    '',
    commonRules(),
    '',
    'DELIVERY:',
    '- ' + branchFrom,
    "- If the branch already exists on origin (rerun), reset onto it: 'git fetch origin && git checkout -B issue-" + c.n + " origin/issue-" + c.n + "' and continue from there.",
    '- Commit(s) per repo conventions (see skills-config).',
    "- Push: 'git push -u origin issue-" + c.n + "'.",
    "- Open the PR with gh pr create — body covers what/why/how it was verified, includes 'Closes #" + c.n + ". Part of #81.', and ends with the repo's standard PR footer. If a PR already exists for the branch, reuse it.",
    "- AFTER the PR exists, run 'git checkout --detach' so follow-up agents can check the branch out.",
    '- If genuinely blocked, open a draft PR with what works and honest notes — never fabricate results.',
    '',
    'Return via StructuredOutput: status (ok|draft|blocked), pr (PR number), branch, notes (<=600 chars, honest, list anything skipped).',
  ].join('\n')
}

function reviewPrompt(c, pr) {
  return [
    'You are an adversarial code reviewer for PR #' + pr + ' (issue #' + c.n + ', "' + c.title + '") in roo-oliv/monodreams.',
    'Work READ-ONLY from the repo root: never checkout branches, never modify files.',
    '',
    "1. Run 'gh pr view " + pr + "' and 'gh pr diff " + pr + "'; 'gh issue view " + c.n + "' for the acceptance criteria.",
    '2. Read docs/CORE_TENETS.md and: ' + c.premises,
    '3. Hunt hard for: violated premises/tenets (ECS purity, one-way-to-do-things, rendering pipeline contracts, module dependency arrows), unmet acceptance criteria from the issue, correctness bugs with a concrete failure scenario, missing or vacuous tests, docs the issue required but the PR skipped. Ignore pure style. A dependency PR that is not merged yet (stacked branches) is NOT a blocker.',
    "4. Post ONE consolidated review comment on the PR via 'gh pr comment " + pr + " --body ...' listing Blockers and Non-blockers (or LGTM if clean).",
    '',
    'Return via StructuredOutput: blockers (ONLY defects that must be fixed before merge; each with file and problem <=300 chars) and nits. Be skeptical but honest — do not invent blockers to seem thorough.',
  ].join('\n')
}

function fixPrompt(c, pr, blockers) {
  const list = blockers.map(function (b, i) { return (i + 1) + '. ' + (b.file ? b.file + ': ' : '') + b.problem }).join('\n')
  return [
    'You are fixing review blockers on PR #' + pr + ' (issue #' + c.n + ') of roo-oliv/monodreams. You are in an ISOLATED GIT WORKTREE.',
    '',
    "1. Run 'git fetch origin && git checkout -B issue-" + c.n + " origin/issue-" + c.n + "'.",
    '2. Address ONLY these blockers — no scope creep:',
    list,
    '3. Context: docs/CORE_TENETS.md, docs/agents/skills-config.md, and: ' + c.premises,
    '4. ' + commonRules(),
    "5. Verify green, commit per conventions, 'git push origin issue-" + c.n + "', post a short PR comment stating what was fixed, then 'git checkout --detach'.",
    'If a blocker is actually wrong (the reviewer misread the code), do not change code for it — explain why in the PR comment and in notes.',
    '',
    'Return via StructuredOutput: status (ok|draft|blocked), pr, branch, notes (<=600 chars).',
  ].join('\n')
}

async function runIssue(c) {
  const ph = 'Wave ' + c.wave
  const impl = await agent(implPrompt(c), { label: 'impl#' + c.n, phase: ph, model: 'opus', isolation: 'worktree', schema: IMPL_SCHEMA })
  if (!impl || !impl.pr) {
    return { issue: c.n, status: 'implement-failed', notes: impl ? impl.notes : 'agent died or was skipped' }
  }
  const rev = await agent(reviewPrompt(c, impl.pr), { label: 'review#' + c.n, phase: ph, model: 'opus', schema: REVIEW_SCHEMA })
  if (!rev) {
    return { issue: c.n, pr: impl.pr, status: impl.status + ' (review-failed)', notes: impl.notes }
  }
  const blockers = (rev.blockers || []).filter(Boolean)
  if (blockers.length === 0) {
    return { issue: c.n, pr: impl.pr, status: impl.status + ' (review clean)', nits: (rev.nits || []).length, notes: impl.notes }
  }
  const fix = await agent(fixPrompt(c, impl.pr, blockers), { label: 'fix#' + c.n, phase: ph, model: 'opus', isolation: 'worktree', schema: IMPL_SCHEMA })
  if (!fix) {
    return { issue: c.n, pr: impl.pr, status: 'blockers-unfixed', blockers: blockers.length, notes: 'fix agent died; see PR review comment' }
  }
  return { issue: c.n, pr: impl.pr, status: fix.status + ' (fixed ' + blockers.length + ' blockers)', notes: fix.notes }
}

const results = []
for (const w of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) {
  phase('Wave ' + w)
  const batch = ISSUES.filter(function (i) { return i.wave === w })
  log('Wave ' + w + ': issues ' + batch.map(function (i) { return '#' + i.n }).join(', '))
  const r = await parallel(batch.map(function (c) { return function () { return runIssue(c) } }))
  results.push.apply(results, r.filter(Boolean))
  const done = results.filter(function (x) { return x.pr }).length
  log('Wave ' + w + ' complete — ' + done + '/' + results.length + ' issues have PRs so far')
}

return { results: results }

| #96 panel group | [#113](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/pull/113) | 2 blockers fixed |

Every PR reports a green full-solution Release test gate (~1275–1316 engine tests + 57–81 CLI tests depending on branch).

**The adversarial loop earned its keep** — three catches worth reading:
- **#83 immediately caught a second lying manifest**: the honesty check found `ui` silently using `rendering-text`'s `DynamicTextComponent` without declaring it — the exact bug class the issue predicted, found on day one. `ui/module.json` now declares it.
- **#92's reviewer found a real engine bug**: text folding interacted with the reveal-count clamp so an ellipsis fold (`…`→`...`) made revealing text truncate *permanently*. Root-caused and fixed with a `ScaleRevealCount` mapping.
- **#90's reviewer caught a replay race**: repeated `waitUntil log` waits matched stale log lines, so a second identical wait passed instantly. Fixed with a consumed-watermark on a sequence-stamped log ring.

**What failed and how it resolved:** the #89 and #91 implementers finished all their work (branch, tests, PR) but crashed emitting their structured return — the same StructuredOutput-cap failure from the level-editor waves — and #97's reviewer died on an API error. Nothing was lost; the only gap was their review stage, and a follow-up workflow (`wf_273cb376-4c9`, watch via `/workflows`) is now reviewing #108/#109/#110 and will fix any blockers on-branch.

**Merge-order guidance when you're ready:** #98 → then #102 (auto-retargets), #100 → then #109 (auto-retargets); the ui family (#107, #111, #112, #113, #110) will each need a trivial rebase on whichever merges first (shared `ui/docs/premises.md` / CHANGELOG appends). One flagged follow-up from #99's review: the repo's own Examples/Demos heads still pin their backbuffer and don't use `WindowFit` yet — the issue scoped adoption to the CLI template, so that's a candidate follow-up issue.

I'll report the three remaining review outcomes when the follow-up workflow completes.

Issue #81 catalogues upstreamable findings from *NFs, Please!* (second full game on
MonoDreams — Papers-Please-style business sim, desktop+web, ~1.6k tests, fully
agent-validated, zero vendored-module edits). On 2026-08-15 it was split into 16 GitHub
sub-issues (#82–#97), all approved one-by-one by the user.

Decisions taken during triage (resolve the catalogue's open questions):
- **#82** collision manifest: declare the `physics` dep (module split rejected/deferred).
- **#83** manifest-honesty CI depends on #82 and must be born-red on pre-#82 code.
- **#88** two-space model (authoring vs render): **first-class in `rendering`**, not just a
  documented pattern; `MapMouse` ships as engine helper.
- **#89** user broadened C2 beyond samplers into a full **presentation scaling policy**:
  overscan-to-clean-scale (bounded tolerance, camera shows more world) → letter/pillarbox →
  stretch with per-layer `Auto|Point|Linear` sampler on `RenderLayer`. Sequences after #88.
- **#93** highlight overlay home = `ui` (not `debug`), generic naming `HighlightComponent`.
- **#96** user asked to generalize "TabSystem" → **`PanelGroupComponent/System`** (exclusive
  panel groups covering tabs, menus, wizards; "none active" first-class; encodes
  park-don't-hide).
- **#97** docs-only bundle (ui double-dispatch premise + audio message-driven cue example) —
  joined because each alone was below the "delivers value on its own" bar.

Split criterion used (user's rule): each sub-issue must deliver value on its own
(sequenceable deps OK); too small → join with peers; still divisible into valuable
deliveries → too big.

Related: [[upstreaming-port-pattern]] (same playbook as the #35 Witch v Necromancer waves,
issues #45–#57).

Session gotcha: text emitted between tool calls (e.g. before AskUserQuestion in the same
turn) sometimes doesn't render in the user's terminal — the user caught it twice. For
approve/reject loops, end the turn with plain text and take approval in chat instead.

content.text:
**All 16 sub-issues of #81 are now implemented, adversarially reviewed, and blocker-free** — PRs #98–#113, every branch with a green full-solution Release test gate.

The three reviews that were pending all found real problems, now fixed:

- **#109 (scaling policy)** — 2 blockers, both doc-vs-behavior mismatches: overscan only covers the fit-binding axis (pillarbars can still appear, and `MapMouse` correctly returns null in them — docs now say so, with a new test), and `PixelPerfect` was over-claimed as identical to the old mode (it deliberately doesn't crop below 1× — claim scoped, 2 tests added). Code was correct; the claims weren't.
- **#108 (RT screenshots)** — 2 blockers with one real root cause: a `??=` latch pinned capture to a **disposed RenderTarget** after the first screen switch or resize, silently killing capture for the rest of the run. Fixed with re-resolution over disposed targets; 4 new tests confirmed failing pre-fix.
- **#110 (docs lessons)** — 1 blocker: the audio example claimed system *order* affects same-frame cue latency, but `AudioSystem` plays `PlaySoundRequest` synchronously at publish time — the claim was false. Replaced with the case where order genuinely matters (component-mutating cues).

**Where this leaves you:**
- **Ready to merge in any order**, except: #98 before #102, #100 before #109 (both drafts auto-retarget to `main` when their base merges); the ui-family PRs (#107, #110–#113) will need trivial rebases on shared `premises.md`/CHANGELOG appends as they land.
- **Two follow-up candidates surfaced by the reviews** (not filed, your call): the repo's own Examples/Demos heads still pin their backbuffer instead of using `WindowFit` (#99's top nit), and #102's honesty check documented a residual Roslyn declaration-phase limit worth knowing about.

Totals for the whole effort: 44 agents, ~7.6M subagent tokens, ~4.2 hours of wall-clock across the two workflows — 16 valuable, sequenceable deliveries from one catalogue issue.

content.text:
Não falhou, não — os dois PRs existem e estão abertos; eles só estão "escondidos" pela mecânica de PRs empilhados do GitHub:

- **Issue #83 → PR [#102](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/pull/102)** — draft, com base no branch `issue-82` (não em `main`)
- **Issue #89 → PR [#109](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/pull/109)** — draft, com base no branch `issue-88`

O motivo de você não vê-los na página dos issues: o GitHub só ativa o vínculo de "Closes #N" (aquela seção *Development* na lateral do issue) quando o PR aponta para o branch default. Como esses dois apontam para `issue-82`/`issue-88` — de propósito, porque o código deles se apoia no código dos PRs #98/#100 —, o vínculo fica dormente e o issue parece "sem PR". Foi uma escolha minha de design do workflow: empilhar em vez de duplicar os commits da base dentro do diff.

**Isso se resolve sozinho:** quando você mergear o #98 (e deletar o branch), o GitHub retargeteia o #102 para `main` automaticamente — aí o "Closes #83" passa a valer e o vínculo aparece no issue. Idem para #100 → #109. Os drafts também foram pensados para isso: sinalizam "não mergear antes da base"; depois do retarget é só marcar ready-for-review.

E ambos passaram pelo ciclo completo de review: #102 teve 2 blockers reais corrigidos (incluindo a descoberta do segundo manifesto mentiroso — `ui` usava `rendering-text` sem declarar) e #109 teve 2 blockers de documentação corrigidos no follow-up.

Se preferir vê-los linkados desde já, posso comentar nos issues #83 e #89 apontando para os PRs — o cross-reference aparece na timeline do issue imediatamente. Quer?

 +(layout) resolution every game number is written in (entity/UI coordinates, HUD and

 +cameras `ViewportManager` hands out. The two spaces **default to being equal**
 +(`RenderScale == 1`), so the model is inert — no pixel, no coordinate and no test moves
 +until a game passes a layout size that differs from its virtual one. What does move is
 +naming: five public shapes now say which space they mean.

 +- **`ViewportManager.ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates(Vector2)` is now
 +  `ViewportManager.MapMouse(Vector2)`**, and its result is a point of AUTHORING space
 +  (`(0,0)` to `LayoutWidth`×`LayoutHeight`), not of virtual space — the same numbers in a
 +  single-space game. `null` still means "the pointer is outside the aspect-fit viewport".

 +  `viewport.MapMouse(mouse)`; keep feeding the result to `Camera.VirtualScreenToWorld`,
 +  which now takes an authoring-space point.

 +  `SetResolution(int virtualWidth, int virtualHeight, int layoutWidth = 0, int
 +  layoutHeight = 0)`** — exactly the constructor's arguments, under the same convention:
 +  a layout dimension of `0` means "same as the render dimension". Both entry points now
 +  validate, where the old setter accepted anything: a non-positive render dimension or a
 +  negative layout dimension throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, and a layout/render
 +  aspect-ratio mismatch throws `ArgumentException`.

 +  `viewport.SetResolution(1920, 1080)`; add the layout pair only to opt into two spaces.

 +  single-space game).

--- a/MonoDreams/rendering/docs/premises.md
+++ b/MonoDreams/rendering/docs/premises.md
@@@ -85,73 -85,49 +85,120 @@@ camera demo, `MonoDreams/camera/demo/Ca
  **Depends on:** "A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its
  destination".
  
++<<<<<<< HEAD
 +## Authoring space and render space are distinct; the scale lives only in the cameras
 +
 +A game has TWO coordinate spaces, both owned by `ViewportManager`.
 +**Authoring (layout) space** — `LayoutWidth`×`LayoutHeight` — is where every
 +game number is written: entity and UI coordinates, HUD/overlay boxes,
 +`Camera.Zoom`, culling extents, and the point `MapMouse` returns.
 +**Render (virtual) space** — `VirtualWidth`×`VirtualHeight` — is the pixel size
 +of the per-pass render targets and of the back buffer. `RenderScale` is the one
 +ratio between them (`VirtualWidth / LayoutWidth`; the two aspect ratios must
 +match, and a mismatch throws), and it is applied in **exactly one place: the
 +per-pass render cameras** — `Camera.RenderScale` multiplies `Zoom` inside the
 +view transform. Nothing else in the engine multiplies a coordinate by it.
 +World passes take `ViewportManager.CreateCamera()`; screen-space passes (UI,
 +HUD, Scroll, …) take `ViewportManager.LayoutCamera` (or `CreateLayoutCamera` for
 +a sub-target) **instead of a null camera**, which is what scales authored UI
 +coordinates onto a larger target. Sizing a render target that must hold a
 +layout-sized region is the one legitimate hand use of `RenderScale`.
 +
 +The two spaces default to being EQUAL (`RenderScale == 1`) — the single-space
 +game — and at that scale `LayoutCamera`'s view matrix is **exactly**
 +`Matrix.Identity`, so passing it everywhere changes no pixel. The model is
 +therefore opt-in: a game opts in by giving `ViewportManager` a layout size that
 +differs from its virtual size, and then a render-resolution move (720p → 1080p)
 +touches the head's two numbers and nothing else — no game coordinate, no UI
 +number, and no coordinate-carrying test moves. Bitmap text is re-rasterized
 +through the camera at the new resolution, so it gains real fidelity from the
 +same font masters.
 +
 +The two entry points that configure the spaces — the `ViewportManager`
 +constructor and `SetResolution` — take the same layout arguments under **one
 +convention**: a layout dimension of `0` means "same as the render dimension"
 +(which is what an unset `GameSettings.LayoutWidth`/`LayoutHeight` is), a negative
 +one throws, and a half-specified pair (`0` beside a real height) resolves to a
 +mismatched aspect ratio and throws as such. `0` never means "single space" in one
 +of them and "invalid" in the other, so a settings object can be forwarded to
 +either.
 +
 +**Why:** hardcoding final-resolution coordinates (buttons at 1720,980; tests
 +asserting pixel positions) makes a resolution change a full recalibration. The
 +`ViewportManager` used to half-support this — one space with a letterbox — which
 +is the worst state: close enough that people assume the second space exists,
 +incomplete enough that the gaps surface mid-project. Keeping the scale in the
 +cameras (rather than sprinkling it over prep systems, layout, and picking) is
 +what makes the opt-in free and the invariant checkable.
 +**Breaks:** applying `RenderScale` a second time anywhere (a prep system, UI
 +layout, a mouse mapping) double-scales that content — visible only once a game
 +actually uses two spaces, so it lands silently. Leaving a screen-space pass on a
 +`null` camera renders authored UI 1:1 into a bigger target: content shrinks into
 +the top-left corner. Reading `VirtualWidth` where an authored number belongs
 +(UI layout roots, HUD/overlay boxes, fit-zoom, frustum outlines) makes that
 +number move with the render resolution — the exact bug the split exists to

## Presentation scaling is a declared policy, resolved in one place

How the window-vs-render-resolution conflict is resolved is a **declared policy**
(`ViewportManager.Policy`, a `PresentationPolicy`), not per-game plumbing and not a
per-layer improvisation. `ViewportManager.Recalculate` runs its chain — in the declared
preference order — over the area left for the game viewport (the window minus any
viewport inset), and the winner produces the ONE `DestinationRectangle` that
`FinalDrawSystem` composites into and `MapMouse` inverts:

1. **Overscan to a clean scale** (`AllowOverscan`) — spend up to `OverscanTolerance` of
   extra scale to reach the clean step ABOVE the aspect-fit scale. The frame then
   overflows the window and its edges leave the screen, which is why that tolerance is a
   GAMEPLAY dial: the honest way to spend it is to render that much more world, and
   `PresentationPolicy.ResolveRenderSize(design, window)` is the other end of the same dial
   — it returns the render resolution at which the clean present has ZERO overflow, so the
   extra scale becomes extra view. That resolution is a boot-time decision (render targets,
   per-pass cameras and the back buffer all follow `VirtualWidth`/`VirtualHeight`), never a
   per-frame one.
2. **Letter/pillarbox at a clean scale** (`AllowLetterbox`) — drop to the clean step BELOW
   the aspect-fit scale and pad with bars, as long as the drop costs no more than
   `LetterboxTolerance`.
3. **Stretch** (`AllowStretch`) — the exact aspect-fit rectangle at a fractional scale: the
   historical present, and the only step that resamples at an arbitrary ratio.

"Clean" is the ladder `CleanScaleSteps` names: whole steps (…, 1/3, 1/2, 1, 2, 3, …), or
whole **and half** steps (…, 1/1.5, 1, 1.5, 2, …) — a half step repeats a fixed 1-2-1-2
pixel pattern rather than an arbitrary one. A fit scale that is already clean is presented
as-is (reported as `Letterbox`; bars only from an aspect mismatch). The chain always
terminates: with `AllowStretch` off the last resort is the clean step below, bars and all.
**Overscan is vetoed while a viewport inset is active** — a frame grown past the game
viewport would paint over the editor chrome reserved around it — but the rest of the chain
still applies inside the inset area.

## Unreleased

<<<<<<< HEAD
### Added — scripted pointer replay in `debug` ([#90](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/issues/90))

`input_replay.json` speaks only named actions, so an entire genre — menus, business sims,
card games, editors — had no scripted-verification story. `PointerReplaySystem` adds the
pointer half: a `debug/pointer_replay.json` plan of `move` / `click` / `wheel` / `type` /
`waitUntil` / `label` commands in authoring-space coordinates, counted in frames, file-gated
and auto-exiting on drain exactly like the input replay. It **injects into the real
`CursorInputComponent`**, so a scripted click exercises the game's actual picking / focus / UI
path. Details in [`MonoDreams/debug/docs/overview.md`](MonoDreams/debug/docs/overview.md)
§ Pointer replay.

Nothing existing changes behaviour, but three source-owned modules gained surface:

- **`debug` now depends on `cursor`** (`module.json`), because the channel injects into
  `CursorInputComponent` rather than simulating one. `monodreams add debug` installs `cursor`
  too.
- **`Logger.LineSink`** (`foundation`) — a static, default-`null`, single-owner tap on every
  emitted message, invoked outside the writer lock. The socket lives in `foundation`, the plug
  in `debug` (the `waitUntil log` predicate), mirroring `GatedSystem.TimingSink`.
- **`TextInputSystem.KeyboardStateProvider`** (`ui`) — the repo's usual `Func<KeyboardState>`
  seam, defaulting to `Keyboard.GetState`, so a scripted `type` reaches a field through the
  system's own key diff.
- **`Cursor.ApplyPose`** (`cursor`) — the per-render-target cursor pose rule, extracted from
  `CursorPositionSystem` so the real mouse and an injected pointer place the cursor identically.
- **`ViewportManager.ScaleVirtualToScreenCoordinates`** (`rendering`) — the exact inverse of
  `ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates`, so an injection channel can fill
  `CursorInputComponent.ScreenPosition` in the backbuffer pixels that field means (chrome
  hit-tests read it raw, and it stays right at `DevicePixelRatio` 2).
- **`GameTestRunner.RunAsync(…, pointerPlan:)`** writes the plan into the run's debug dir.
||||||| 342dba6
=======
### Breaking — presentation scaling is a declared policy ([#89](https://github.com/roo-oliv/monodreams/issues/89))

How the frame reaches a window that is not the render resolution is now declared once, on
`ViewportManager.Policy`, and resolved in one place: **overscan** to a clean scale →
